stops.title: The question
stops.text: QLoRA showed you how to fine-tune a model on a small GPU. Now let's see what a small model that can look at pictures is made of. TinyLLaVA Factory is not a new model. It is a codebase for building and training small vision-language models, with language models from 450 million to 2.7 billion parameters. For a fine-tuning project it does two jobs: it explains clearly how an image becomes something a language model can read, and it already ships LoRA and QLoRA recipes.

stops.title: Two paths into one model
stops.text: Here is the whole model in one picture. The image goes through a vision tower, such as SigLIP, and then a small connector, a two-layer network, that turns image features into visual tokens. The question goes through the chat template and becomes ordinary text tokens. Both streams enter one small language model, which writes a text answer. Now notice the grey boxes. There is no voice input, no video and no speech output. For your task, a speech-to-text model must turn the spoken question into text first.

stops.title: The real problem is code
stops.text: So what problem does the paper solve? In the original LLaVA code, the vision tower and the connector live inside the language model class. Swapping any part means editing model code, and mistakes are easy. TinyLLaVA Factory makes the three parts equal partners, each built by its own factory from a shared base class. You change a vision tower or a language model by changing one line of a config file. That design choice drives everything else in the paper.

stops.title: What the model learns from
stops.text: This small diagram matters more than it looks. Each training sample, an image plus a conversation, is turned into a prompt, tokenized, and given labels. Only the answer tokens count in the loss; the system message, the image tokens and the question are masked. Each language model family needs its own template for this. When you build your dataset of at least three hundred examples, getting this format right is half the battle, and a wrong template quietly ruins fine-tuning.

stops.title: Who trains, who stays frozen
stops.text: A training recipe is a switch for each part: frozen, fully trained, or trained through LoRA adapters. In the paper, the vision tower is always frozen. The base recipe first trains only the connector to align images with words, then trains the connector and the language model on instructions. The last row is your case: a frozen, four-bit language model with small LoRA adapters, using the recipes the codebase provides. The paper itself reports no LoRA results, so your numbers will be new.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: The reproduced models score slightly better than the original TinyLLaVA paper, which is the paper's main evidence. This chart shows why modularity pays off. Swapping CLIP for SigLIP, one config line, raises TextVQA by 3.3 to 5.5 points for every language model, and TextVQA is the benchmark closest to asking about a document photo. One caveat: not every metric agrees, since MME drops with SigLIP for two models. Always check more than one metric in your own comparison.

stops.title: What you take from it
stops.text: So here is your plan if you choose this model. It reads text and one image, so put a speech-to-text model in front for the voice part. Start from the smallest variant, check its real size on the model hub, and use QLoRA with fp16 on a free T4. Freeze the vision tower and put adapters on the language model. For fairness, compare speaker groups, and separate transcription errors from answer errors. Next, SmolVLM shows how to squeeze vision into an even smaller model.
